summary: Kosei Mizutani was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Ryukoku University (~1951–1956) and Bukkyo University (doctorate, 1979). He served as Bukkyo University's president (~1978–1989) and chaired the boards of Bukkyo Kyoiku Gakuen (~1999–2011) and Tokai Gakuen (~2001–2014).

Kosei Tada was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo. He held a post at Taisho University (~1975–2008) and served as board chairman of the Society for Buddhist Cultural Studies (attested 2004).

Active in Buddhist studies and philosophy, Kosen Imakita studied under Togai Fujisawa, Kyokuso Hirose, Daisetsu Shoen, and Gisan Zenrai at Shokoku-ji and Sōgen-ji. He served at the Ministry of Religion (~1872–1875) and was abbot of Engaku-ji (1875–1892).
Koshin Suzuki is an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar who completed doctoral studies at Taisho University. He also served as a researcher at Taisho University (attested 1995–1998).

Koshiro Tamaki worked in Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy, earning his doctorate from the University of Tokyo in 1959. He was a professor at the University of Tokyo (1964–1976), Tohoku University (~1976–1978), and Nihon University (1979–1986).

Kosho Kawamura worked in Buddhist studies and Indology, studying at Toyo University under Giyu Nishi, Nichijin Sakamoto, Shunkyo Katsumata, Koshiro Tamaki, and Yoshiro Tamura. He served as a researcher at Toyo University (~1975–1994) and honorary professor at Nava Nalanda Mahavihara (~2001).

Kosho Uchiyama was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who completed a master's at Waseda University and studied under Kodo Sawaki (1941–1965). He taught at Miyazaki Catholic Seminary and served as abbot of Antai-ji (1965–1975).
Koshu Itahashi was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Sendai Daiichi High School, the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy (~1944–1945), and Tohoku University (~1949–1953) under Teruji Ishizu.

Kotatsu Fujita worked in Buddhist studies and Indology, earning a BA at the University of Tokyo and studying at Harvard. Supervised by Shoson Miyamoto and Hajime Nakamura, he served at Osaka University (~1962–1968) and as professor at Hokkaido University (~1968–1985).
Koun Kajiyoshi was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo (~1927–1930) and held a post at Taisho University.
Koyo Sakaino worked in Buddhist studies and history/archaeology. He held posts at Toyo University (~1904–1923) and Komazawa University, and founded the Bukkyo Seito Doshikai.
Koyo Shimizu is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Shoko Takeuchi and served as a part-time lecturer at Ryukoku University (attested 1995).

Koyu Tamura specialized in Buddhist studies and Japanology, earning a master's and doctorate from the University of Tokyo. He held posts at Nishogakusha University (1965) and Toyo University as associate professor (1972–2000).

Kozen Shaku was a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology who studied under Senmyō. He served as chief priest at Gyokuri-ji (1870–1881) and Sange-ji (1882), and taught at Nagano Prefectural Northern Chugakurin (1881).

Kozui Otani worked in Buddhist studies, Iranian/Central Asian studies, and history/archaeology, studying under Keiun Maeda and at Gakushuin University. He served as the 22nd Abbot of Nishi Hongan-ji (1903–1914) and was a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society (~1902–1948).
Kripa Shankar Shukla was an Indology and history/archaeology scholar who held posts at the University of Lucknow (until 1959 and attested in 1976).

Krishna Kamal Bhattacharya was an Indology scholar who studied at Sanskrit College and University and Presidency University (~1857–1860). He held posts at Presidency University (1862–1872) and Surendranath College (1891–1903).

Krishna Kanta Handiqui was an Indologist who completed M.A. degrees at the University of Calcutta and the University of Oxford. He served as principal of Jagannath Barooah College (1930–1948) and vice-chancellor of Gauhati University (1948–1957).

Krishna Mohan Banerjee worked in Indology, linguistics, and religious studies, studying at Presidency University, under Alexander Duff (~1831–1832), and at Bishop's College (1836–1839). He served at Hare School (~1829–1831) and Bishop's College, Kolkata as second professor (1852).

Krishnacharya Tammannacharya Pandurangi was an Indology and philosophy scholar. He served as Professor of Sanskrit at Bangalore University, Honorary Director of the Dvaita Vedanta Studies and Research Foundation (attested 1997), and Upakulapati at Poornaprajna Vidyapeetha (attested 1997).
